name: Russia on the Page, the Stage and the Score
description: Pushkin to Shostakovich: how Russian novelists, playwrights, composers and painters built a culture that outlived tsars and commissars alike.

checkpoints.name: Fortress and window
checkpoints.note: The Moscow Kremlin is first fortified in the twelfth century and grows into the seat of Russian power. In 1703 Peter the Great founds Saint Petersburg on marshland by the Neva as a new capital that looks out toward Europe, and the city later becomes a centre of the arts.

checkpoints.name: The golden age begins
checkpoints.note: Alexander Pushkin, born in 1799, sets a standard for Russian poetry and prose. Nikolai Gogol writes comic and strange stories. Napoleon's invasion of 1812 leaves a memory later used in fiction, and Ivan Turgenev and Fyodor Dostoevsky, born in 1818 and 1821, soon follow.

checkpoints.name: Novels, ballets and plays
checkpoints.note: Tolstoy's War and Peace appears in 1869, and Dostoevsky's novels probe guilt and belief. Tchaikovsky writes Swan Lake (1877), the 1812 Overture (1880) and The Nutcracker (1892). Chekhov brings sharp, quiet plays to the stage, and Sergei Rachmaninoff, born in 1873, grows into a leading pianist-composer.

checkpoints.name: Revolutions and the new
checkpoints.note: The revolution of 1905 and the revolution of 1917 reshape the country, and Pravda, founded in 1912, becomes a Bolshevik paper. Wassily Kandinsky, born in Moscow, pioneers abstract painting, while Igor Stravinsky's ballet The Rite of Spring shocks its Paris audience in 1913.

checkpoints.name: Under Soviet rule
checkpoints.note: The Soviet Union is founded in 1922. Battleship Potemkin (1925), directed by Sergei Eisenstein, is admired abroad for its editing, while Sergei Prokofiev and Dmitri Shostakovich write major works while working under the watch of the state. The Soviet era ends in 1991.
